summary: Extends Kerberos PKINIT with an opaque blob the KDC can validate, to ensure the client currently holds the private key during initial authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: The guard gives you a fresh code to sign to prove you have the key now, not that you copied an old signature.

questions: why does pkinit need a freshness token
how does kerberos prevent pre-generated pkinit requests
subtitle: A KDC-issued freshness token that proves a Kerberos PKINIT client holds its private key right now, not just that it used it once.

tldr.problem: In PKINIT with Diffie-Hellman, the client signs its request before contacting the KDC, so requests can be pre-generated with future times and used later without the private key.
tldr.mechanism: The KDC sends an opaque freshness token in a KRB_ERROR, and the client includes it in the signed PKAuthenticator of its next AS request.
tldr.outcome: The KDC can confirm the client had the private key when it built the request. The change is optional for a realm until the realm requires it, and until then the pre-generation risk remains.

today: RFC 8070 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends PKINIT from RFC 4556.

sections.title: Why Freshness Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 4556 (PKINIT) defines two ways to use public-key cryptography in Kerberos pre-authentication: Diffie-Hellman key exchange and public key encryption. The encryption scheme is less common. RFC 5349 specified only ECDH for elliptic curves, so it cannot be used for encryption. Encryption also needs certificates with an encryption key, which many deployed smart cards lack.

With Diffie-Hellman, the client uses its private key only to sign the AuthPack, before any traffic goes to the KDC. A client can therefore generate requests with future times in the PKAuthenticator and send them later. Unless the time falls outside the certificate's validity period, the KDC validates the request and returns a Ticket-Granting Ticket the client can use without the private key.

So the client proves only prior use of the key, not current possession. Proving current possession needs signed data that the client could not have predicted.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine signing a stack of permission slips in advance and handing them out later. Anyone holding a slip looks like you, even if your pen is long gone.

sections.title: The Message Exchange
sections.content:
The design borrows the flow password-based Kerberos often uses: the client first sends an AS request with no pre-authentication, and the KDC answers with an error carrying what is needed to continue. Here the KDC supplies a token.

  1. The client sends a KRB_AS_REQ with no PA_PK_AS_REQ and a freshness token request.
  2. The KDC replies with a KRB_ERROR carrying a freshness token.
  3. The client extracts the token and includes it in a new KRB_AS_REQ.
  4. The KDC validates the request as in RFC 4556 and also validates the token.
  5. The exchange continues as in RFC 4120 and RFC 4556.

To ask for a token, the client adds a padata element of type PA_AS_FRESHNESS with an empty octet string. The KDC answers with error code KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and a PA_AS_FRESHNESS element holding the token in the METHOD-DATA object. The client treats the token as an opaque blob and places it in the freshnessToken field of the PKAuthenticator, so it falls inside the signed data.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the guard for a fresh code, the guard gives you one, you sign it, and you hand it back. A signature made earlier cannot contain a code that did not exist yet.

sections.title: Padata Type and the Extended PKAuthenticator
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new pre-authentication data type, PA_AS_FRESHNESS, with padata-type value 150.

It also extends the PKAuthenticator from RFC 4556 with an optional freshnessToken field, tagged [4], an OCTET STRING that carries the PA_AS_FRESHNESS value as received from the KDC. The comments in the ASN.1 say it MUST be present if the KDC sent one. The existing fields stay: cusec and ctime for replay prevention, a randomly chosen nonce, and paChecksum, a SHA1 checksum over the KDC-REQ-BODY.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a new empty box on the form labelled "fresh code goes here". Because it sits inside the signed part, it cannot be changed or filled in earlier.

sections.title: How the KDC Validates and Retries
sections.content:
If the realm requires freshness and the request has no token, the KDC MUST return a KRB_ERROR with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED and a PA_AS_FRESHNESS element holding a token.

If a token is present, the KDC validates the request normally and then checks the token in an implementation-specific way. An invalid token makes the KDC MUST return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_EXPIRED (RFC 6113), whose e-data holds a METHOD-DATA object with a valid token. A client that receives such an error with a new token SHOULD retry with it.

Since freshness tokens are validated by KDCs in the same realm, standardizing their contents is not an interoperability concern.
sections.plainLanguage: If your code is too old, the guard says so and hands you a new one. You try again with that.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability Notes
sections.content:
The token SHOULD include signing, encrypting or sealing of data from the KDC, so it can be authenticated and not tampered with. Tokens guarantee the client had the key when constructing the AS-REQ. They need not be single-use or bound to a specific exchange. The token is opaque so KDC implementers can add functionality, as long as tokens expire so the freshness guarantee holds.

Because clients treat the token as opaque, changing its contents does not affect existing clients. Clients SHOULD NOT reuse tokens across exchanges, and a client that does not retry with a new token may be incompatible with some KDCs.

Implementers may allow both token-based and legacy exchanges while clients are upgraded. Until a realm requires freshness tokens, the existing risk of pre-generated PKAuthenticators remains.
sections.plainLanguage: The code has to expire, or it would be just another old slip. Until the guard insists on codes, someone with an old slip might still get in.

messages.label: AS-REP
messages.note: After the KDC validates the request and the token.
